summary: Hafsa bint Umar (RA) was a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and a daughter of the second Caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA). She holds the singular distinction of being entrusted with the first compiled Mus-haf (written copy of the Quran) by her father, making her a central figure in the preservation of the Quranic text. She was known for her intelligence, piety, and frequent fasting.
biography:
Hafsa bint Umar ibn al-Khattab al-Qurashiyyah al-Adawiyyah was born in Makkah around 605 CE, five years before the beginning of prophethood according to Ibn Sa'd's al-Tabaqat al-Kubra. Her father was Umar ibn al-Khattab (RA), who would become the second of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and her mother was Zaynab bint Madh'un, from the Banu Makhzum. She grew up in a household that would later become one of the most prominent in early Islamic history.

Hafsa accepted Islam early alongside her family. She was first married to Khunays ibn Hudhayfah al-Sahmi (RA), a companion who had participated in both the Hijrah to Abyssinia and the Hijrah to Madinah. Khunays fought at the Battle of Badr and was seriously wounded, subsequently dying from his injuries in 2 or 3 AH. Hafsa was thus widowed at a young age, and her father Umar sought a husband for her among the senior companions. He approached both Uthman ibn Affan (RA) and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA), but both declined at that time — Uthman because he was mourning his own wife Ruqayyah bint Muhammad (RA), and Abu Bakr out of knowledge that the Prophet ﷺ had already expressed his intention. The Prophet ﷺ then married Hafsa himself in 3 AH (approximately 625 CE), uniting the families of two of his closest companions and cementing one of the defining social bonds of the early Muslim community.

Among the Mothers of the Believers, Hafsa was distinguished by her literacy and her intense devotion to worship. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' that she was among the very few women in early Arabia who could read and write, and she was deeply committed to fasting and night prayer. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said of her: 'Hafsa is a woman of much fasting and prayer' (Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, Vol. 8). This devotion colored her entire life — she maintained a rigorous schedule of worship even into her later years.

The most enduring legacy of Hafsa (RA) lies in the preservation of the Quran. After the Battle of Yamama in 12 AH, in which a large number of huffadh (Quran memorizers) were martyred, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) commissioned Zayd ibn Thabit (RA) to compile the Quranic text from written fragments and memorization. When this first compiled Mus-haf was completed, Abu Bakr entrusted it to Umar ibn al-Khattab. Upon Umar's death, it passed into the custody of Hafsa. This was not a casual arrangement: Hafsa's custody meant the authoritative written reference remained within the household of someone known for both literacy and trustworthiness. When Uthman ibn Affan (RA) later undertook the standardization of the Quranic text during his caliphate in 25 AH, he sent to Hafsa requesting the Mus-haf, from which the authorized copies were produced. After the standardized copies were distributed, the original Mus-haf was returned to Hafsa, and it remained with her until her death. Ibn Sa'd and al-Dhahabi both record this chain of custody in detail, confirming that it is one of the most well-documented episodes of early Islamic scholarship.

Hafsa lived through the entire period of the first four caliphs — Abu Bakr, her father Umar, Uthman, and Ali (RA). She witnessed the extraordinary expansion of the Muslim world and the political tensions of the late Uthmani and early Alid periods. In keeping with the Athari scholarly approach, the details of her political positions during the period of fitnah are recorded where they are transmitted by reliable narrators, but she is remembered above all for her spiritual qualities and her unique role in Quranic preservation.

Hafsa (RA) died in 45 AH (approximately 665 CE) in Madinah, during the governorship of Marwan ibn al-Hakam. She was buried in the Baqi' cemetery. Al-Dhahabi places her among the most distinguished of the Mothers of the Believers in terms of scholarship and worship. She narrated approximately 60 hadith in the major collections, among them several on prayer, fasting, and the Prophet's personal conduct.

Classical scholars including Ibn Sa'd, al-Dhahabi, and Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in al-Isabah fi Tamyiz al-Sahabah honor Hafsa as one of the most learned women of her generation and as an indispensable link in the transmission of the Quran to the ummah.
